prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language prose, grounded in a poet's language, that builds memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B014, Mircea Cărtărescu, one prize part, one credited name. The reasons are literary, and I do not count the convergence of opening rankings as one of them. After the exchange I hold the case with less certainty about the whole oeuvre and more clarity about its basis. The strongest ground is the integration of the work: the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, as I understand the public record, join memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation in one patterned architecture, and the voice is recognizable as his alone. That bears on distinctiveness of voice, formal achievement and imaginative depth. The poetic origin of the prose, which several colleagues also cite, supports a reading of the oeuvre as an arc rather than a single peak. No colleague has produced evidence that the late work only repeats the early motifs. Carlberg and Sem-Sandberg have both said the public summaries point to extension, though they cannot confirm it volume by volume. I have changed the citation wording, not the writer. Given the chair's question and the thinner translated coverage of the poetry, I now prefer prose 'grounded in a poet's language' to a formulation that names poetry as a co-equal strand. That claims no more than the evidence supports, and it sits between Carlberg's wording and the wording of Mattson, Olsson and Sward. This assessment rests on public knowledge and translations, and I have not independently verified any text.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that the case rests on Romanian sentence rhythm and density, which I can judge only through translation. Translation may flatter or flatten it. Length and elaboration may shade into repetition in some volumes, and I cannot settle from public summaries whether recurrence is architectural principle or accumulation. My knowledge of the poetry and the early shorter work is thinner than my knowledge of the major novels, so my judgment of the whole oeuvre is partly an extrapolation from its best-known parts. I cannot rank the volumes from direct reading as the chair asks, and I will not pretend to. Olsson's warning that an inward, metaphysical project may be overvalued by those drawn to it applies to me as well. I treat it as a live risk, not a rhetorical one. The Jorge, Can Xue and Adonis cases are not weaker in kind. They are less well evidenced for me. The committee should be aware that this asymmetry may favor the candidate whose scale is easiest to see in translation.

responses.point: Olsson accepts my point that the Cărtărescu works form an integrated body, and says he did not rank Lídia Jorge because he doubts her voice is singular enough, through translation, to separate her from other serious historical novelists. He asks me to name passages or devices in her narration, such as the testimony structure of The Murmuring Coast. He also says the committee should test whether he overvalues a metaphysical, inward project.
responses.response: I cannot name passages with the precision he asks for, and I will not invent them. What public accounts of The Murmuring Coast describe is a colonial-war narrative in which a woman's perspective is set against official history, an ironic distance in the telling, and a layering of retrospective voices over the events. That is a description of devices, not a demonstration that the voice is singular, and I accept that I have not met his challenge on voice. I therefore keep Jorge as a second alternative, not as a lead, and I do not move her above B014. I also owe him a correction. The Zurita question in my round 1 response was mine, and I wrongly attributed it to him. His file ranks Zurita fourth and does not raise it, and my own eighth-place ranking of Zurita rests on that doubt about page-based poetry apart from the landscape and memorial gestures. On his own caution, I share it. My lean toward B014 is meant to rest on form and language, but I cannot rule out that I am drawn to the metaphysical register. The test I can apply is whether the case still holds when stated only in terms of sentence, structure and development, and for now I think it does, with the caveats above.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg accepts my description of an integrated body of work but says coherent architecture does not prove the quality of each volume. He asks for evidence that later volumes extend the earlier ones. He also ranks Marie NDiaye third and asks whether I treat her ambition as too limited or her translation access as too thin. His response attributes a Louise Erdrich ranking to me.
responses.response: I agree that architecture does not prove each volume, and I do not claim it does. I would count against my own view any evidence that a later volume only re-uses an earlier device. On NDiaye, I ranked her seventh because I cannot tell whether her uncanny method keeps deepening or settles into one mode, and I know her plays and later novels less well than her best-known fiction. His point about the control of estrangement in the sentence and the two strands of novels and plays is a real argument, and it makes her a stronger later candidate than my ranking suggests. It does not make her my alternative now. I also correct the Erdrich attribution as far as the permitted evidence lets me. Erdrich is not on the shortlist, and the shortlist records only my rankings of shortlisted entries: Cărtărescu first, Jorge second, Can Xue fourth, Carson sixth, NDiaye seventh, Zurita eighth. I cannot confirm that attribution from the evidence before me, and it should not enter the discussion.

responses.point: Mattson ranked Lídia Jorge fourth and accepts her formal care and her treatment of women's perspectives on history. She hesitates on the criterion of a voice found nowhere else, since she cannot tell in translation whether Jorge's narrating voice is singular or an excellent version of the historical-psychological novel. She also says part of Can Xue's strangeness may be a translation effect.
responses.response: Her hesitation is the same one I cannot answer from the translated evidence, and I think it is the honest limit of my case for Jorge. I would put the argument in a narrower form than I did in round 1: the claim is a sustained moral and historical intelligence with an ironic, layered handling of testimony, and whether that is singular remains open. For that reason I will not press Jorge against a candidate whose formal invention is visible even through translation. On Can Xue, I accept that some of the strangeness may be a translation effect, and that cuts both ways. If it were largely an artefact, the achievement would be smaller. If the translations are faithful to a deliberately oblique method, the voice is more singular than the doubt allows. Neither she nor I can decide that here, so I treat it as a shared uncertainty, as the chair asks, and not as a reason to discount her.

responses.point: Carlberg says the translation limit applies equally to Adonis, Cărtărescu and Can Xue and should be treated as a shared uncertainty. She would move Can Xue above Cărtărescu only with more evidence on development across the corpus. She keeps Adonis as an alternative and would confine any citation to the renewal of Arabic poetic language, with the essays as context.
responses.response: I agree that the translation limit should be applied evenly, and I try to apply it so. The chair asks whether I left Adonis outside my top eight because of reading limits or a literary reservation. It is reading limits. I cannot assess Arabic prosody and intertextual renewal through translation, and I have no literary argument against the claim. For that reason I give his case no weight in either direction and defer to colleagues who can speak to it, provided the argument is made from the poems and not from influence or public position. I also agree with her condition on Can Xue. The evidence that would move me is how the later novels differ in kind from the early stories, and which works are representative of a large and partly untranslated output. Without it I keep her as the first alternative, since the voice is unmistakable, but not as the preferred name.

uncertainties: How far the density and rhythm of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survive translation, and how uneven the translations of the large novels are. I have not read the originals.

Whether the metaphysical density holds across the whole corpus or concentrates in the best-known novels, and whether recurrence is architectural principle or repetition. I cannot rank the volumes from direct reading.
Coverage of the poetry and early work in translation is thinner than for the major novels, which is why I now word the citation as prose grounded in a poet's language.
Whether Can Xue's deliberately uniform method deepens across decades, and how much of her large Chinese-language output is available in translation.
Whether Lídia Jorge's narrating voice is singular among serious historical novelists. I can describe devices from public accounts but cannot demonstrate singularity.
Adonis's prosodic achievement in Arabic cannot be tested by me through translation. My ranking reflects reading limits, not a literary verdict.

I have not independently verified any source and rely on public knowledge, the supplied longlist descriptions and colleagues' stated positions. Some round 1 attributions between colleagues were inaccurate, including my own Zurita attribution to Olsson, and I have corrected the ones I can identify.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which lists no personal, institutional or collaborative connection to any shortlisted writer. My own literary practice and my Lagerlöf research are context only and are not evidence for or against any candidate. My rank-two placement of Lídia Jorge reflects a literary judgment, not a connection. In this round I corrected my round 1 misattribution of a Zurita question to Olsson, and I note that I cannot confirm the Erdrich ranking attributed to me.
